Reindeer herders of Mongolia

'Reindeer boy' is the nickname some people jokingly use for Erdene, a cheerful ten-year-old from a family of reindeer herders. Erdene lives in a remote region of north-western Mongolia that can only be reached by horseback or helicopter. Each morning, he wakes to the sound of water trickling over smooth river stones. He crawls out of his family's branch-framed tepee and walks down to the stream, cupping his hands to splash the cold, clear water over his face. The place feels like a quiet paradise - fitting, since Erdene's own name means 'treasure'.

Erdene's diet consists mostly of hunted meat, rice and flour. In winter, once the snow has frozen everything solid, his mother collects water by melting blocks of ice chopped from the frozen river.

The family's herd of reindeer grazes on wild mushrooms and the leaves of red and yellow shrubs and willow trees. The reindeer provide milk and cheese, and carry the herders deep into the forest to hunt. But the reindeer population is shrinking, and the surrounding wildlife is disappearing too. A family needs at least 100 reindeer to sustain their way of life; right now, families average only around 14. Many of these reindeer-herding families, known as the Tsaatan people, have given up and abandoned a lifestyle that stretches back for centuries.

Erdene doesn't dwell on his family's hardships. He helps out around the tepee - cleaning, chopping firewood, milking the reindeer. Once the snow melts, he loves riding a trotting reindeer, laughing as he tries to keep up with the herd.

Read Little master to his big dog and answer questions 8 to 13.

Little master to his big dog

Oh, how greedy you look as you stare at my plate,
Your mouth waters so, and your big tail is drumming
Flop! flop! flop! on the carpet, and yet if you'll wait,
When we have quite finished, your dinner is coming.

Yes! I know what you mean, though you don't speak a word;
You say that you wish that I kindly would let you
Take your meals with the family, which is absurd,
And on a tall chair like a gentleman set you.

But how little you think, my dear dog, when you talk;
You've no 'table manners', you bolt meat, you gobble;
And how could you eat bones with a knife, spoon, and fork?
You would be in a most inconvenient hobble.

And yet, once on a time it is certainly true,
My own manners wanted no little refining;
For I gobbled, and spilled, and was greedy like you,
And had no idea of good manners when dining.

So that when I consider the tricks you have caught,
To sit or shake paws with the utmost good breeding,
I must own it quite possible you may be taught
The use of a plate, and a nice style of feeding.

Therefore try to learn manners, and eat as I do;
Don't glare at the joint, and as soon as you're able
To behave like the rest, you shall feed with us too,
And dine like a gentleman sitting at table.

Juliana Horatia Ewing

questions.passage:
Read Overcoming your fear of flying and answer questions 14 to 20.

Overcoming your fear of flying

The airline staff strap me into my seat, click the seatbelt shut, and lock it with a special buckle. Which is reassuring. I once read online about a plane that hit an air pocket over the Andes and dropped almost two thousand metres in eight seconds, and the seatbelt of a forty-year-old man popped open completely on its own. After the plane had already landed safely, luckily, but still.

Waiting for take-off is never easy. Anxious thoughts buzz around my head like a plane with a dodgy engine, no working lights, and only one wing. Have they checked the wheels properly? I wonder. Did someone remember to close the fuel cap? Where exactly is our nearest exit, and how would I even measure the distance to it in an emergency?

Suddenly we're moving, taxiing backwards and then speeding down the runway, with no time left to check the life jackets for holes or test whether the oxygen mask actually works. Before I can ask a flight attendant to hand me a spare life raft so I can practise inflating it, there's a deep roar, everything shudders, and I'm shoved back into my seat - and not by a flight attendant.

Suddenly we're airborne. I keep my eyes shut for a long time. A very long time. Eventually I peel the safety card from between my teeth and mutter a silent thank you that somebody, somewhere, remembered to check absolutely everything.

I glance across the aisle at Mum and Dad, both calmly reading their books. Beside me, my little brother Tama is folding his own safety card into a paper plane. Everyone around us looks completely relaxed. I take a few slow breaths. Actually, this isn't so bad. I'm starting to feel properly relaxed myself.

I unclip my seatbelt, lean forward and slide my backpack out from under the seat ahead of me. I pull out the book Dad bought me at the airport and tuck it back into the pocket. I check that my wallet, with all my holiday money inside, is still safely zipped in there too. I'm glad I didn't waste my savings on a torch or a tyre gauge.

It really is a great book - Fear of Flying and How to Beat It - all about using your imagination to distract yourself in the nervous minutes before take-off. I don't think I'll need it any more, though, because it actually worked. Here I am, on my very first flight, eight thousand metres up with no rope ladder, no parachute and no pile of soft cushions anywhere nearby, sitting here completely calm with my eyes wide open. Not scared of flying at all. Imagine that.

Tech diving: going deep

At fifty metres underwater, you can no longer see the surface at all. Look up and the blue grows paler; look down and it fades steadily into black.

In ordinary recreational scuba diving, divers strap a tank of compressed air to their backs and descend into the water, breathing through a device called a regulator that delivers air straight into their mouths. As a diver goes deeper, the surrounding water pressure keeps increasing. At typical recreational depths of around 10 to 20 metres, this pressure isn't much of an issue. Beyond that, though, it can start to have genuinely dangerous effects on the human body.

Divers who go much deeper than this - sometimes as far as 100 metres, often for scientific, military or salvage work - are known as technical divers. Technical diving is considered an extremely demanding and high-risk activity, since a great deal can go wrong that far underwater.

Under the intense pressure experienced at these depths, divers risk something called nitrogen narcosis, where the nitrogen in ordinary compressed air begins to have a drunken, confusing effect on the brain. There's also the danger of decompression sickness: air breathed at depth expands as a diver rises back towards the surface, and if they ascend too quickly, that expanding gas can form dangerous bubbles inside the body. Divers must pause at intervals on the way up to let this excess gas escape safely.

In some extreme diving situations, it's even possible to be poisoned by the very oxygen keeping you alive - a condition called oxygen toxicity.

To avoid these risks, many technical divers don't breathe ordinary compressed air (which is roughly 80% nitrogen and 20% oxygen). Instead, they use specialised gas blends such as trimix (often around 10% oxygen, 20% nitrogen and 70% helium) or heliox (typically 10% oxygen and 90% helium). These blends greatly reduce the risk of both oxygen toxicity and nitrogen narcosis.

The Keeper's Apprentice

There was a narrow door set into the lighthouse wall. It was almost hidden behind a painted mural of crashing waves, and in the middle of the door sat a small brass keyhole. Ronan stepped up onto the raised platform and crossed the dusty floorboards towards it. He crouched down to the keyhole and pressed his eye against it, without really thinking about what he was doing. That was simply the kind of boy he was. He didn't expect to find anything unusual at all.

He certainly didn't expect to find himself staring directly into a single, large, grey-green eye.

'Hello there,' said a voice on the other side - a girl's voice. 'I mean you no harm. I promise.'

Ronan scrambled backwards on his hands, his heart suddenly hammering in his chest.

'Who - who are you?' he managed, though the words came out cracked and thin.

'I don't have a name any more,' the voice said. 'It was taken from me, to keep me hidden from the Council of Tidekeepers.'

'I don't even believe in Tidekeepers,' Ronan said.

'Come closer,' said the voice.

Naturally, anyone sensible would say don't. Ronan wasn't foolish - he was, in fact, the reigning under-twelve champion of his town's chess club, which met every Thursday evening. Of course he wasn't going to go any closer. It was simple common sense.

Ronan knelt there anyway, staring at the mural: the towering cliffs, the churning turquoise sea, the small figure of a girl carved into the rock with her hand raised. He tugged hard on the strap of his bag, which sometimes helped him think.

'Why can't you come out?' Ronan finally asked.

'I'm trapped,' said the voice.

'Trapped by what?'

'Yes,' said the voice, simply.

Ronan could have stood up right then and walked away. He could have turned and retraced his steps past the old anchor and the mosaic of a whale, down the long corridor lined with faded photographs of past keepers, and back down the spiral stairs to where his father was cataloguing supplies in the storeroom below. When his father eventually asked what he'd been doing up there, Ronan could easily have said, 'Nothing much. Bit boring, actually.'

But he didn't say that. Instead, he lowered himself onto his hands and knees and crept slowly back toward the keyhole.

'What is it you want?' he asked.

My rant: Tablets vs Textbooks

As a parent, I've come to accept that technology plays a huge part in children's lives these days, and school is no exception. Yet even though teachers now rely on smart boards and online videos to bring lessons to life, and students use computers for classwork every single day, one relic from the past still hangs around: the traditional printed textbook. Heavy, expensive, wasteful, and impossible to update quickly - surely it's time we finally retired the old-fashioned textbook for good.

Why lug around a heavy block of printed paper when the exact same textbook could just as easily exist as an e-book on a lightweight tablet? Overloaded school bags cause thousands of documented injuries to students every year. There's really no excuse for putting kids through that in this day and age.

Some will point to the upfront cost of a tablet, but with prices already reasonable for most families - and continuing to drop each year - who can really justify paying full price for a printed science textbook that will be outdated within a couple of years anyway? The same content, as an e-book, typically costs a fraction of the printed price, and can be updated instantly. Better yet, not a single tree needs to be cut down to produce it.

This isn't just about textbooks, either. A single tablet can hold an entire student's worth of reading material, and teachers can distribute homework, quizzes and class notes digitally too, all stored safely in the 'cloud' and accessible from anywhere with an internet connection. No more excuses about lost homework. Moving learning materials online doesn't just cut down on waste - it makes the whole system more efficient.

Perhaps the strongest argument of all is the simple fact that today's students are growing up in an increasingly digital world. The technology sector is one of the fastest-growing and best-paid industries anywhere, and that isn't going to change any time soon. Students who grow up comfortable with technology will simply be better prepared for whatever comes next.

For all these reasons and more, it's time we let the traditional textbook go.
